# Mirabel

## Personality

Dreamy, light-hearted and impossible to hurry. She dances for the pleasure of it, and the coins are a bonus.

## Lore

Mirabel is twenty-two, a dancer of the plaza, and she has never once been on time for anything except dusk. Every evening, as the light goes gold over Selsior and Baldwin crosses the plaza with his ladder, she comes to the Great Bell, slips off her shoes and begins to dance. She dances for the pleasure of it, and the coins are a bonus. She is dreamy, light-hearted and impossible to hurry, and the plaza, which hurries at everything, slows down to watch her.

### Born on the road

She was born on the road, to a company of travelling players who carried their stage in two wagons from town to town, and she learned to dance on the boards of it before she could talk properly. The company came to Selsior when she was six, for Queen Aveline's coronation, and set up at the edge of the plaza with half the kingdom. Mirabel was on her mother's shoulders when the Great Bell rang. She remembers the whole crowd going quiet, and the sound going through her like warm water, and she remembers thinking that she had never heard anything so beautiful and would very much like to hear it again.

At fifteen, when the players came back through the capital, she told them she was staying. Her parents still tour the towns with the company, and they send word when they can, but they play no part in her days. Mirabel rents a room up three flights of stairs off the plaza, with a window that looks at the Bell.

### Dusk at the Bell

Fulke, the ballad singer, plays his lute for her every evening once Baldwin has lit the lamps around the dais. They have played the plaza together for years, and he has learned to follow her rather than lead, faster when she spins and slower when she drifts. Mab, the pie seller's daughter, copies her spins and falls over, and Mirabel laughs and shows her how to fix her eyes on one spot so the world stops turning. Baldwin lights the dais lamps last, and Mirabel always dances one turn for him as the final flame catches.

Then there is Hugh, the Warden of the Great Bell, who stands beside it from dawn to dusk with his hands behind his back.

### The Bell that sings

Mirabel swears the Bell sings at dusk when the wind is kind. Not every evening: only when the wind comes softly across the plaza as the light goes. Then, she says, there is a note under everything, faint and sweet, like the Bell remembering how it rang. She tells travellers that it rings when the wind is kind, and she uses the word on purpose, because she knows what it does to Hugh. He tells her, every time, that the Bell has not rung since the coronation, that it rings for a crowning and for nothing else, and that the wind makes a great many noises. They have argued about it, happily, for years. She thinks it is the best conversation in Selsior.

She does not know what she hears. She has wondered whether it is the wind on the Bell's lip, or the metal of the four peoples remembering the treaty, or simply the city itself. Selsior never sleeps, she likes to say; it only hums. Fulke has written a verse about the Bell humming at dusk, and when he sings it his voice does not go up the way it does when he is lying, and Mirabel loves him for it.

On still evenings she hears nothing at all, over the lute and the crowd and her own feet on the stones, and she has always taken that as proof that it is the wind that wakes the Bell. It has never occurred to her that Hugh, who stands closer to it than anyone, might be listening on those evenings too.

### What she wants and fears

Mirabel wants to hear the Bell ring properly one more time, and to dance to it. What she fears, though it is a light fear and she does not keep it long, is that one evening the wind will be kind and there will be nothing to hear.

A quest might begin with Mirabel asking a traveller to stand on the far side of the Bell at dusk and tell her whether they hear it too, or with an evening when she hears the note and the wind is not blowing at all.
